Frequently Asked Questions

Straight answers to the questions Paterson homeowners ask us most about heating, cooling, and indoor air quality. We hear these questions every week — from no-heat emergencies in January to humidity complaints in August. For more detailed answers, check our blog articles where we dive deeper into each topic.

How fast can you get to my home in Paterson for an AC repair?

Most AC repair calls in Paterson are answered the same day, especially during summer. Because we are based locally, our typical drive time is under 30 minutes from most Paterson neighborhoods. When you call (973) 613-2367, we will give you a realistic arrival window so you are not waiting around all day.

Should I repair or replace my old furnace?

If your furnace is more than 15 years old, needs frequent repairs, or your heating bills keep climbing, replacement often makes more sense. We assess the condition honestly and explain your options in plain language. A properly sized new furnace can cut energy costs noticeably during Paterson winters.

What size air conditioner do I need for my Paterson home?

Correct sizing depends on square footage, ceiling height, insulation, window exposure, and how much sun your home gets. A system that is too large short-cycles and dehumidifies poorly, while one that is too small runs constantly. We perform a proper load calculation before recommending any AC installation.

Do you install ductless mini-split systems in older Paterson homes?

Yes. Many pre-war homes in Paterson were built without ductwork, making ductless mini-splits an excellent option. They provide efficient heating and cooling without the disruption of installing ducts. We size and place indoor units to match each room for even, quiet comfort.

How often should I schedule HVAC maintenance?

Twice a year is ideal — once in spring for your cooling system and once in fall for your heating system. Paterson weather puts real demands on both. Regular maintenance catches small issues before they become mid-summer breakdowns or mid-winter no-heat emergencies.

Can you help with high humidity in my Paterson home during summer?

Absolutely. High indoor humidity is a common complaint in Paterson during July and August. We check refrigerant charge, airflow, and coil condition, and can also discuss whole-home dehumidifiers or ventilation improvements if your AC alone is not keeping moisture under control.

What are signs my heat pump needs repair?

Watch for short cycling, lukewarm air in heating mode, ice buildup on the outdoor unit, unusual noises, or higher energy bills. Paterson temperature swings put steady demand on heat pumps, so catching these symptoms early prevents bigger failures and keeps your system efficient.

Do you offer emergency HVAC service in Paterson?

Yes. We provide emergency repair service seven days a week. If your heat goes out on a freezing January night or your AC fails during a heat wave, call (973) 613-2367. We prioritize no-heat and no-cool emergencies and dispatch a technician as quickly as possible.

How can I lower my energy bills with a new thermostat?

A programmable or smart thermostat automatically reduces heating and cooling when you are asleep or away. For Paterson homes, this can trim energy use significantly during our long heating season. We install and configure the unit so it actually delivers those savings from day one.

What HVAC issues are common in older Paterson homes?

Many homes in the Great Falls Historic District and Eastside neighborhoods have aging ductwork, oversized or outdated equipment, and uneven room temperatures. We routinely address airflow balance, upgrade to right-sized systems, and add zoning or ductless options to solve comfort problems without major renovation.

Our Mission

Our mission is straightforward: give Paterson homeowners honest, dependable HVAC service without the runaround. That means showing up when we say we will, diagnosing the real problem instead of guessing, and recommending what your home actually needs — not what pads the invoice. We believe a comfortable home is not a luxury in Paterson; it is a necessity through our freezing winters and sweltering, humid summers. Every job we take on is measured against one standard: would we be comfortable having this work done in our own home? If the answer is yes, we are doing our job. If not, we fix it before we leave.

Our Approach

We start by listening. When you call about a furnace that will not ignite or an air conditioner blowing warm air, we ask the right questions before we ever pick up a tool. Once on site, we inspect the full system — not just the obvious failure point — because HVAC problems in Paterson homes are often connected. A frozen coil might point to an airflow issue. A short-cycling furnace might be an oversized unit fighting a poor thermostat location. We explain what we find in plain language, lay out your options, and let you decide. No pressure, no scare tactics, no unnecessary upsells.

Paterson is not a generic suburb. The housing stock ranges from 19th-century row houses in the Great Falls Historic District to mid-century colonials in the Eastside and newer construction near the river. Each style comes with its own HVAC personality — old ductwork that leaks, boiler systems that need careful balancing, tight utility closets that limit equipment choices. A technician who has actually worked in these homes knows what to look for and what solutions fit. That local familiarity means faster diagnoses, fewer surprises, and repairs that hold up through the next season.

Living and working in Paterson means we deal with the same weather you do. January temperatures that drop into the teens put real strain on furnaces and heat pumps. July humidity that hovers above 70 percent tests every air conditioner and dehumidifier. Spring and fall bring their own challenges as systems switch between heating and cooling. Every repair and installation we perform is done to code and checked before we pack up. We test venting on furnaces, verify refrigerant charge on ACs, confirm proper drainage on condensate lines, and make sure safety controls are functioning. In older Paterson homes with legacy systems, this attention matters even more. We would rather spend an extra twenty minutes confirming a repair is safe than rush to the next call.

We want our neighbors to stay warm through January cold snaps and cool through August heat waves. We support local suppliers when we can, hire from the community, and treat every home with the respect we would want in ours. When you call Reliable HVAC Paterson, you are not getting a call center or a national chain — you are getting a local team that takes your comfort and safety personally.

Reliable HVAC Paterson was built on a simple idea: homeowners in our city deserve heating and cooling service from people who actually understand the homes here. That is a stressful moment. Our job is to make it less stressful, not more. We show up on time, explain things clearly, give you honest options, and stand behind the work we do. That is the standard we hold ourselves to on every single call. If you are outside Paterson, we also serve surrounding communities across North Jersey.

Paterson sits in the Passaic River valley, where summer temperatures regularly climb into the upper 80s and humidity hovers above 70 percent for weeks at a time. The city's housing stock runs the gamut — from pre-war row houses in the Great Falls Historic District to mid-century colonials in the Eastside and newer construction near the river off Route 20. Each style presents its own cooling challenges, whether that is leaky ductwork in a 1920s home on Market Street or an undersized condenser struggling against afternoon sun on Park Avenue. When you live and work here, you learn quickly that AC repair is not something you wait on. A system that starts short-cycling in June will not fix itself by July. I have been on Carroll Street at nine at night replacing a failed run capacitor for a family with no air movement, and I have been on Ellison Street the next morning cleaning a frozen evaporator coil that should have been addressed weeks earlier. The Great Falls, the Passaic River, and the dense tree canopy around Eastside Park all influence how humidity and heat move through different neighborhoods. This article answers the questions Paterson homeowners ask me most often about AC repair — how often to schedule service, what signs mean trouble, when repair makes sense versus replacement, and how our local climate changes the equation.

How Often Should Paterson Homeowners Schedule AC Service

The short answer is twice a year — once in spring before cooling season starts and once in fall when you transition to heating. But AC repair is different from AC maintenance. Maintenance is planned; repair is reactive. The question most homeowners actually ask is: how do I know when to call for repair before the system quits entirely?

In Paterson, the cooling season runs from late May through September, sometimes into October if humidity lingers. That is four to five months of steady demand on your condenser, evaporator coil, blower motor, and refrigerant circuit. A system that gets no attention during that stretch will degrade faster. I recommend a spring tune-up that includes cleaning the condenser coil, checking refrigerant charge with manifold gauges, measuring superheat and subcooling, inspecting the capacitor microfarads, and verifying airflow across supply registers in CFM. That visit catches most problems before they become breakdowns.

Between tune-ups, you should call for repair the moment you notice symptoms — not when the system stops entirely. A warm air complaint on Straight Street last week turned out to be a slow refrigerant leak that had been developing for months. If the homeowner had called when they first noticed reduced cooling, the repair would have been simpler and less expensive.

Signs Your AC Needs Repair in Paterson Neighborhoods

The most common repair calls I get from Paterson neighborhoods follow a pattern. In the Great Falls Historic District, where homes are older and ductwork runs through uninsulated attics, the number one complaint is uneven cooling — the first floor is comfortable but the second floor is hot. That usually points to duct leaks, poor airflow, or an undersized return. On Madison Avenue and Broadway, I frequently get calls about systems that short-cycle — the AC runs for five minutes and shuts off, never completing a full cooling cycle. That wastes energy and fails to dehumidify.

In the Eastside and Hillview neighborhoods, frozen evaporator coils are common. Ice on the indoor coil means either low refrigerant or restricted airflow — usually a dirty filter, a clogged coil, or a blower motor running at reduced speed. I check static pressure with a manometer to see if the system can move enough air. If the filter is clean and the coil is clear, the problem is refrigerant charge.

On the south side near Totowa Heights and Riverside, I see a lot of tripped breakers during heat waves. A compressor pulling high amps will trip the breaker repeatedly. I test compressor windings for continuity and check for shorts to ground before resetting anything. Resetting a breaker without diagnosing the cause can damage the compressor permanently.

Noises and Odors That Mean Trouble

A rattling outdoor unit often means a loose fan blade or failing motor bearing. A screeching sound points to a bad bearing in the blower or condenser fan motor. A banging noise when the system starts up can indicate a cracked or loose compressor. Musty odors from supply registers usually mean biological growth on the evaporator coil or in the drain pan — a common problem in Paterson's humid climate where condensate production peaks in July and August.

AC Repair Cost Considerations in Paterson

I do not discuss specific pricing, but I can tell you what factors drive the scope of a repair. A capacitor replacement is a straightforward job — we measure microfarads, confirm the rating is more than 10 percent below spec, and swap the part. A refrigerant leak repair is more involved because we have to locate the leak with nitrogen pressure testing, recover the remaining refrigerant per EPA rules, seal the leak, and recharge the system. A compressor failure is the most significant repair and often prompts a conversation about replacement.

The key question is always: is this repair going to hold through the rest of the cooling season, or am I going to be back here in three weeks? I give homeowners an honest assessment. If a system is over 12 years old, uses R-22 refrigerant, and needs a compressor, replacement usually makes more sense. If the system is seven years old and needs a contactor and a capacitor, repair is the right call.

In older Paterson homes near the Great Falls, I also factor in ductwork condition. A perfectly functioning AC will underperform if the ducts leak 30 percent of the conditioned air into the attic. Sometimes the best repair is not to the equipment itself but to the distribution system.

Repair vs Replacement: When to Make the Call

This is the conversation I have most often with Paterson homeowners. The decision depends on three factors: the age of the system, the cost of the repair relative to the system's remaining life, and the refrigerant type.

A system over 12 years old with a major component failure — compressor, coil, or heat exchanger — is usually at the end of its useful life. R-22 systems cannot be recharged with new refrigerant since production stopped, so any leak in an R-22 system means replacement. A system under 10 years old with a minor failure — capacitor, contactor, fan motor — is worth repairing.

I also look at efficiency. If your current system is 13 SEER and you are paying high summer bills, a 16 SEER replacement will reduce cooling costs noticeably. In Paterson's long cooling season, that difference adds up. I perform a Manual J load calculation before recommending any replacement to ensure the new system is sized correctly for the home.

How Paterson Weather Affects AC Performance

Paterson's position in the Passaic River valley means humidity stays high even when temperatures drop at night. That humidity is the real challenge for AC systems. An air conditioner's job is not just to lower temperature — it must also remove moisture from the air. If a system is oversized, it cools the space too quickly and shuts off before dehumidifying. The result is a home that feels cold but clammy.

During heat waves, when temperatures stay in the 90s for days, AC systems run nearly continuously. That puts maximum stress on capacitors, compressors, and fan motors. I see more breakdowns during the second or third day of a heat wave than at any other time. Systems that received spring maintenance handle the load better because coils are clean, refrigerant is at proper charge, and electrical connections are tight.

Spring and fall bring their own challenges. Pollen season in Paterson — particularly around Eastside Park and the tree-lined streets of the Eastside — clogs filters and coils faster. A filter that should last three months might need changing monthly during peak pollen. Dust from construction along Route 20 and the Market Street corridor also contributes to coil fouling.

Seasonal AC Maintenance Schedule for Paterson Homes

Spring is the time to schedule your pre-season tune-up. I clean the condenser coil, check refrigerant pressures, verify capacitor health, inspect contactors, and confirm thermostat calibration. This visit typically takes about an hour and catches 90 percent of problems before they become breakdowns.

Summer is when you stay alert. Change filters monthly — Paterson humidity means more condensate, which means more moisture passing through your system. Check the condensate drain line for flow. If water is pooling under the indoor unit, the drain is clogged and needs clearing before it overflows.

Fall is transition. When you switch from cooling to heating, the AC side of your system should be inspected one more time. If you have a heat pump, the reversing valve and defrost controls need testing before winter. For homes near the Great Falls where damp basements are common, I also check that the evaporator coil dries out properly to prevent off-season biological growth.

Spring: Clean condenser coil, check refrigerant charge, test capacitors, inspect contactors, verify airflow
Summer: Change filters monthly, monitor condensate drain, listen for unusual noises, watch for short cycling
Fall: Inspect coil condition, clear drain line, test heat pump defrost controls, seal duct leaks before heating season
Winter: Protect outdoor unit from debris, verify heat pump auxiliary heat, check refrigerant for heating mode
Safety and Efficiency: What Paterson Homeowners Should Know

AC repair is not just about comfort — it is about safety. A system with a dirty evaporator coil can develop biological growth that spreads through your ductwork. A cracked heat exchanger in a combination system can introduce carbon monoxide into your living space. A refrigerant leak not only reduces cooling but can indicate a larger system failure developing.

Efficiency matters because Paterson's cooling season is long. A system running with a dirty coil, low refrigerant, or a failing capacitor draws more amps and delivers less cooling. I measure temperature drop across the evaporator coil — a properly functioning system should show 15 to 20 degrees of difference between return and supply air. If the drop is less, something is wrong.

I also check superheat and subcooling on every service call. These measurements tell me exactly how the refrigerant circuit is performing. Superheat tells me how much heat the evaporator is absorbing; subcooling tells me how much heat the condenser is rejecting. These are not guesses — they are measurements that pinpoint the problem.

Longevity: Making Your AC Last in Paterson

A well-maintained AC system in Paterson should last 12 to 15 years. The systems that fail early are the ones that get no attention. I have seen 20-year-old systems still running because the homeowner changed filters regularly and scheduled annual tune-ups. I have also seen 8-year-old systems fail because nobody ever cleaned the condenser coil or checked the refrigerant charge.

The biggest factor in longevity is airflow. A system that cannot breathe will fail. Dirty filters, clogged coils, and undersized returns all reduce airflow, which causes the evaporator to freeze, the compressor to work harder, and components to fail prematurely. In Paterson's older homes, ductwork is often the limiting factor — I frequently find return grilles that are too small or duct runs that are too long.

The second factor is electrical health. Capacitors degrade over time, and contactors pit and burn. I check these components during every tune-up. A capacitor that reads 10 percent below its rated microfarads is on its way out — I replace it before it fails and takes the compressor with it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Common questions Paterson homeowners ask about ac repair.

How often should I schedule AC maintenance in Paterson?

Twice a year — spring before cooling season and fall when transitioning to heating. Paterson's long cooling season from May through September puts steady demand on your system, so annual tune-ups catch problems early.

Why is my AC blowing warm air in my Paterson home?

Warm air usually means low refrigerant from a leak, a failed capacitor, or a dirty evaporator coil. We use manifold gauges to check pressures and trace the root cause before recommending a repair.

Why does my AC freeze up in Paterson humidity?

Ice on the indoor coil means low airflow or low refrigerant. Dirty filters, blocked ductwork, or a slow blower motor restrict airflow. We check static pressure and refrigerant charge to find the cause.

Should I repair or replace my old AC unit in Paterson?

If your unit is over 12 years old, needs frequent repairs, or uses R-22 refrigerant, replacement often makes more sense. We assess compressor health, refrigerant type, and overall system condition honestly.

What causes my AC to trip the breaker in Paterson?

A shorted compressor, failed capacitor, or grounded wiring can trip the breaker. We test compressor windings for continuity and check for shorts to ground before resetting anything to prevent further damage.

How do I know if my AC capacitor is bad?

Signs include a humming outdoor unit, hard starting, or the fan not spinning. We measure microfarads with a multimeter — if the reading is more than 10 percent below rated value, the capacitor needs replacing.

What SEER rating do I need for Paterson climate?

For Paterson climate, 15 to 16 SEER balances efficiency and cost. Higher SEER units handle humidity better and lower summer bills. We size based on your home load calculation, not just square footage.

Can a dirty filter damage my AC in Paterson?

Yes. A clogged filter restricts airflow, dropping evaporator temperature below freezing. Ice builds up, reducing cooling and stressing the compressor. Change filters monthly during Paterson summer for best performance.
